subject: Modern History
name: Modern History, Units 1 and 2
about: VCE, Between the wars, and the world after 1945
syllabus: VCE History Study Design (from 2022), Modern History Units 1 and 2

chapters.title: Empires and the First World War

points.title: The end of empires
points.brief: From the late 1800s, empires competed for land and power while new nation states emerged, as in Meiji Japan and the unification of Germany and Italy.

points.title: The world after the First World War
points.brief: The war ended empires, killed millions and left Europe in debt, setting up the tensions of the next two decades.

points.title: The Fourteen Points and self-determination
points.brief: Woodrow Wilson's plan for peace promoted the right of peoples to rule themselves, which shaped new borders and raised hopes in colonies.

points.title: The Treaty of Versailles
points.brief: The 1919 peace treaty made Germany accept blame, pay reparations, give up land and cut its army, which many Germans resented.

points.title: The League of Nations
points.brief: Set up to keep peace through collective security, it lacked the United States and an army, and failed to stop aggression in the 1930s.

points.title: Liberal democracy
points.brief: Government by elected representatives, with rights, the rule of law and several parties, under strain in the interwar years.

points.title: Communism in the Soviet Union
points.brief: Under Lenin and then Stalin, the Communist Party ruled alone, owned industry and farms, and used terror against opponents.

points.title: Fascism in Italy
points.brief: Mussolini's Fascists took power in 1922, promising order and national glory, and built a one-party state.

points.title: Nazism in Germany
points.brief: Hitler's Nazis rose amid the Depression and came to power in 1933, ending democracy and persecuting Jews and others.

points.title: The Weimar Republic
points.brief: Germany's democracy from 1919 faced hyperinflation, uprisings and the Depression before the Nazis ended it.

points.title: The Great Depression
points.brief: The 1929 Wall Street crash led to a world slump, mass unemployment and support for extreme parties.

points.title: The New Deal
points.brief: Franklin Roosevelt's programs from 1933 used government spending and new agencies to fight the Depression in the United States.

points.title: The road to the Second World War
points.brief: Aggression by Germany, Italy and Japan, and appeasement by Britain and France, led to war in 1939.

points.title: The 1920s and modern life
points.brief: Cars, radio, cinema and jazz changed daily life in the 1920s, and young people challenged older ways.

points.title: Women between the wars
points.brief: Many women won the vote and new freedoms in work and dress, though most still faced limits at home and work.

points.title: Challenges to the social order
points.brief: Strikes, protests and new movements challenged class, race and gender roles between the wars.

points.title: Modern art and culture
points.brief: Movements such as Expressionism, Cubism and Surrealism, and new film and music, reflected and shaped a changing world.

points.title: Propaganda and control
points.brief: Totalitarian states used propaganda, censorship, youth groups and secret police to control what people thought and did.

points.title: Art and culture under dictatorship
points.brief: Dictatorships controlled art, film and writing to spread their ideas and banned what they saw as dangerous.

points.title: Persecution of minorities
points.brief: The Nuremberg Laws stripped Jews of rights in Nazi Germany, leading to violence and, in the war, the Holocaust. Sinti and Roma people were also persecuted.

points.title: The Great Purge
points.brief: In the late 1930s Stalin's secret police arrested, imprisoned and killed huge numbers of Soviet citizens accused of disloyalty.

points.title: White Australia
points.brief: The Immigration Restriction Act of 1901 kept most non-European migrants out of Australia for decades.

points.title: Origins of the Cold War
points.brief: After 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union, with clashing ideologies, became rival superpowers.

points.title: Yalta and Potsdam
points.brief: The 1945 conferences redrew borders and divided Germany, and the disagreements there fed growing distrust.

points.title: Communism and capitalism
points.brief: The Soviet Union's one-party state and planned economy stood against the United States' democracy and free markets.

points.title: The United Nations
points.brief: Founded in 1945 to keep peace, it also took on human rights, economic and social problems and refugees.

points.title: The Iron Curtain and Europe divided
points.brief: Europe split into a Soviet-controlled east and a western bloc, with Germany and Berlin divided.

points.title: Containment and the Truman Doctrine
points.brief: The United States aimed to stop communism spreading, with aid such as the Marshall Plan and alliances such as NATO.

points.title: The arms race
points.brief: Both superpowers built nuclear weapons, leading to the idea of mutually assured destruction.

points.title: Proxy wars
points.brief: The superpowers fought through others in Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan rather than directly.

points.title: Divided Berlin
points.brief: Berlin was split after 1945. The Wall built in 1961 stopped East Germans leaving until it fell in 1989.

points.title: Dissent in the Soviet bloc
points.brief: Uprisings in Poland and Hungary in 1956 and the Prague Spring of 1968 were put down by Soviet power.

points.title: The Cuban Missile Crisis
points.brief: In 1962 Soviet missiles in Cuba brought the world close to nuclear war, until both sides stepped back.

points.title: The end of the Cold War
points.brief: Reform in the Soviet Union, the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the Soviet collapse in 1991 ended the Cold War.

points.title: Decolonisation
points.brief: After 1945 many colonies in Asia and Africa won independence, sometimes peacefully and sometimes through war.

points.title: The civil rights movement in the United States
points.brief: African Americans used boycotts, marches and court cases to end segregation and win voting rights.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander rights in Australia
points.brief: Campaigns such as the Freedom Ride and the 1967 referendum challenged discrimination and pushed for rights and land.

points.title: The women's movement
points.brief: From the 1960s women campaigned for equal pay, legal rights and control over their own lives.

points.title: Anti-war protest
points.brief: Opposition to the Vietnam War brought mass protest in the United States and Australia.

points.title: The end of apartheid
points.brief: Protest inside South Africa and pressure from abroad ended apartheid, leading to elections in 1994.

points.title: Methods of protest and change
points.brief: Movements used non-violent protest, legal action, media and sometimes violence, with different results.

points.title: Resisting change
points.brief: Governments and groups with power used laws, police, propaganda and violence to resist movements for change.

points.title: Measuring change
points.brief: Historians judge how far a movement reached its goals, and what changed or stayed the same in the short and long term.
